_note: The merged MyThuso Control Tower: one portal where the Control Tower workspace and the back office used to be two (docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md §5.1, §6, §10 Phase 3). This file holds the portal's shape as data — its categories in the plan's order, the tabs inside each, where every tab and section of the two old surfaces now lives, the context the address carries, the parallel run's two sentences, and every written empty state and refusal a category screen shows that no other contract already owns. It holds no status and no count: a service's state is read from packages/catalog/control-tower-overview.json and the assistant's health route, a device fact from packages/catalog/vitals.json and packages/catalog/devices/, a queue's state from packages/catalog/clinical-review-queue.json and packages/catalog/protocols.json#governance, and a pack's gates from packages/catalog/compliance-pack.json. Web only: docs/control-tower-tab-inventory.md places every one of these surfaces in the web application, no native screen reads this file, and so it has no generator and no line in the generated-files registry, like packages/catalog/vitals.json.
_statusWhy: The portal is in the tree and held by tests/control-tower-portal.spec.ts on both viewports. Built is not accepted: gate G15 stays open until whoever runs the cutover signs docs/control-tower-cutover.md, and nothing here is a real service.
name: MyThuso Control Tower
_statusVocabularyWhy: One vocabulary for every service state the portal shows (§5.2). It lives in the Overview's contract, which the plan authored first; this file points at it rather than keeping a second copy, and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails a portal file that declares its own list of status words.

buildVocabulary.sentence: In the tree, held by tests.
Declared in a contract, not built.
Built but blocked on a named gate.
A contract the work must author.

_buildVocabularyWhy: The plan's §2 words for how far a thing is built, used exactly. A copy of a Markdown table no screen can read, so scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds each row to docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md §2 word for word.

previewPicker.sentence: No session, permission or admin layer exists behind this portal. Every category is open to anybody who opens this address, which is why nothing here acts on anything real. The fifteen admin layers are gate G16.
previewPicker.why: The role switcher is a preview picker and the portal is where a reader could most easily mistake a category list for access control. The capability's own sentence says the switcher authenticates nobody; this one says what that means for the portal.

params.label: Site
params.sentence: There is no site registry, so there is one site and it is all of them. The address carries it so a link keeps working the day a second one exists.
params.why: §5.2 asks for site in the address. A site list with invented hospitals in it would be read as customers.

params.label: Period
params.sentence: The period is carried in the address so a link opens the same view. No screen here reads a metered figure yet, so changing it changes no number; a screen that would be scoped by it says so.
params.why: A period control that silently changed nothing would be a control lying about what it does.

params.label: Tenant
params.sentence: No tenant. A tenant in the address is ignored until a tenancy contract creates one.
params.why: docs/control-tower-cutover.md: a tenant parameter is refused until a tenant exists.

context.why: Which category, which tab, which site and which period all live in the address and nowhere else — no storage, the same rule the role follows (apps/web/src/lib/roles.ts) — so the address is bookmarkable and Back returns to the previous tab.

tabs.blurb: Every tab and section of the Control Tower workspace and the back office, and where it is now.

tabs.label: Audit exports
tabs.blurb: Check a date range against the bound an admin sets, before the export route would be asked for it.

tabs.blurb: Devices by ward, bed, class and status, what needs attention, and the cohorts they fall into.

tabs.label: Provisioning

tabs.label: Engine overview

tabs.blurb: Every language-model provider the plan names, the one that is configured, where it runs, and the key controls a vault would stand behind.

tabs.label: Intelligence
tabs.blurb: The five reasoning levels, which conversation may reach which, and the ceilings nothing on this screen can raise.

tabs.label: Knowledge
tabs.blurb: The clinical and the non-clinical corpus, the three external sources, and the lock on the clinical half.

tabs.label: Engine compliance
tabs.blurb: The compliance pack, the audit extract, the kill switch, and where each provider processes what it is sent.

tabs.label: API Registry
tabs.blurb: Every external API the platform talks to, or has been asked to, as a card with its honest state.

tabs.label: Configuration
tabs.blurb: Sites, wards, beds, staff, roles, branding and integrations, and every setting the engines work to.

tabs.label: Cost allocation

_categoriesWhy: The first eleven are the plan's order (§5.1), which scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds to the tree drawn there. Clinical oversight, Catalogue and Growth follow because docs/control-tower-tab-inventory.md moves them in and the plan's tree does not name them; they are appended rather than interleaved so the plan's order is not reargued by a screen.

roleLanding.why: docs/control-tower-cutover.md: ?role=control-tower opens the portal on Dispatch & Incidents and ?role=back-office on Overview, for one release cycle with the notice below.

_legacyAddressesWhy: Every tab and section docs/control-tower-tab-inventory.md marks moved or merged, and where it lands. scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds this list to the inventory's tables in both directions and to the two old surfaces' own tab lists, so a tab cannot be dropped on the way in. Neither old surface put its tab in the address, so the addresses that must keep working are the two roles; a category parameter naming any old tab or section (?role=back-office&category=operations) resolves here as well, so a link written the old way lands on the new place.

decisions.sentence: The link that opened Configuration on the field-safety settings hung off the back office's Operations tab. It now sits under the Incidents tab, beside the board whose waiting times those settings decide.
decisions.decidedBy: Phase 3 build, 24 September 2026, for acceptance at the cutover sign-off
decisions.why: docs/control-tower-tab-inventory.md left this undecided and docs/control-tower-cutover.md made it a blocker. The settings are how long the safety desk waits; the desk is the Incidents tab. Recorded here so the person who signs the cutover accepts or changes it rather than discovering it.

notice.sentence: The Control Tower workspace and the back office are one portal now. Everything either of them held is in a category here.
notice.shownWhen: A role address with no category in it — ?role=control-tower or ?role=back-office as it was bookmarked before the merge — for one release cycle.
notice.why: docs/control-tower-cutover.md, the addresses that must keep working: the old address lands on the portal with a one-line notice that the two surfaces are now one.

legacy.sentence: This screen is kept for comparison while the Control Tower changes over. Do this in the Control Tower.
legacy.linkLabel: Open this in the Control Tower
legacy.why: docs/control-tower-cutover.md, the parallel run: the legacy surfaces stay reachable by an explicit address, read-only, with every action refused in this sentence. The sentence is the cutover plan's own, word for word.

rollback.sentence: Pointing control-tower and back-office at their old shells again is one change to apps/web/src/lib/roles.ts (each role's surface) and a deploy. The old shells stay in the bundle for the parallel run so that rollback is a small revert rather than a rebuild.

settingsPage.what: Every settings page in the Control Tower looks the same: one head, tinted section cards, a row per setting with the value in force under it, one save bar, and the same arrival.
settingsPage.why: The founder found the settings pages looking different from one another. The words here are the only sentence the shared pattern adds; everything else on a settings page is its own contract's.

loading.sentence: Getting this screen ready. It was not downloaded until you opened it.
loading.why: Every category is a dynamic import, so a patient never pays for it. A panel that fills is announced; a panel that is filling says so rather than showing a blank region (§5.2).

overview._healthTimeoutWhy: Long enough for a slow connection to the one route the Overview reads live; short enough that the service row settles as disconnected rather than spinning. A timeout is not a clinical number.
overview.whatChangedWindow: No release date is recorded anywhere this screen can read — deploys happen at a terminal on the server — so what changed is the feature map's Delivered entries from the Control Tower plan's Phase 0 onwards, newest first.

overview._whatChangedWhy: The Overview contract reads what changed from docs/FEATURE-MAP.md's Delivered sections, which no screen can read: the file is most of a megabyte of Markdown. So each item is a copy of one Delivered heading, and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds every heading to the feature map word for word, every ref to a file that exists, and the list to newest first.

devices.fleetEmpty: The real-device allowlist holds {real} devices, and the DPIA that would let one onto it is {dpia}. No device belongs to a fleet, so there is no ward, bed, class or status to group one by.
devices.attentionEmpty: Nothing needs attention, because nothing is being watched. Low battery, offline too long, calibration overdue, firmware behind and verification pending are each an indicator below; a fleet with no device raises none of them.
devices.cohortEmpty: No cohort exists. A cohort is the devices of one model on one firmware, and there are {real} real devices to put in one.
devices.bulkRefusal: No bulk action is offered. There is no device to act on, and a bulk action on a fleet of none would be a button that says it did something.
devices.synthetic: The kit registry the desk works today holds synthetic instruments only. It is under Dispatch & Incidents, Incidents, and the Device Lab simulator is in this category's More tools; neither is a real device and neither is on the allowlist.
devices.provisioningEmpty: Nothing can be provisioned. The real-device allowlist holds {real} devices and the DPIA is {dpia}, so a device that completed all four steps would still be refused at the first reading.

steps.label: Discover
steps.sentence: Find the device on one of the transports below, in trust order. Discovery proves nothing: a device answering on a radio is not a device somebody is holding.

steps.label: Pair
steps.sentence: Complete the transport's possession proof. A pairing without it is refused, and no device whose class may carry clinical weight pairs by a transport's 'just works' mode.

steps.label: Assign
steps.sentence: Give the device to whoever holds it between readings — a site, a ward and bed, a nurse's kit or a patient. No site, ward or bed exists to assign one to.

steps.label: Verify
steps.sentence: Check the device's own credential before its first reading is accepted. No device holds a credential yet, so there is nothing to verify against.

devices.startRefusal: There is no Start button. Provisioning is proposed: no pairing route exists, and a wizard that walked somebody through four steps to a refusal would be wasting their afternoon.
devices.allowlistEmpty: No device class is on this deployment's allowlist: the real-device allowlist holds {real} devices and the DPIA is {dpia}.
devices.gate: A device class cannot be enabled at a site until the DPIA covers it. This is a gate, not a delay.
addingAClassRequires: The tier it is supported at
A physiological range for each reading type it reports
A security review confirming its credential model
devices._addingAClassRequiresWhy: §5.4 View 3, the plan's list of what a class needs before it is added. The physiological range is a plausibility bound in packages/catalog/vitals.json's sense, never a threshold: a threshold is a clinical rule and waits on a ratified review-queue entry (packages/catalog/devices/thresholds.json).
devices.enableRefusal: Nothing on this screen enables a device class. A class joins the allowlist by a deliberate, reviewed edit to packages/catalog/vitals.json after the DPIA covers it, never by a button.
devices.thresholdsEmpty: No device class carries a threshold. Every threshold is a clinical rule and waits on a ratified entry in the Clinician Review Queue.

gilbertone._statusWhy: Built in Phase 4 (24 September 2026): seven sub-screens in the tree, held by tests/gilbertone-admin.spec.ts on both viewports. An eighth, Speech settings, was added on 28 September 2026 and the same day the founder had the Voice screen folded into it — "Voice and Speech settings are duplicated; collapse them into one place, Speech settings" — so the category is seven sub-screens again, with the merged one second where Voice stood. Built is not live, with the exceptions the founder decided: on 27 September 2026 the Save as default and Play that the Voice screen carried and the merged screen keeps, each with its own dated live record in actions below, and on 28 September 2026 the knobs' Save beside them; and, from the founder's instruction of 28 September 2026 ("I need to be able to control all these aspects, I am the owner"), the key, switch, test and log actions on Model Providers and the API Registry, each carrying a founder record and enabled only inside the founder's signed-in session, through the assistant service's founder routes. Each sub-screen reads contracts and, on the Overview, two routes that answer booleans; every other action it draws is disabled beside the gate that holds it, and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails the build the day a gate closes while its action still has nothing behind it.
gilbertone.sentence: Built, and administering three things. These seven screens read the assistant's contracts and ask its health and status routes for their booleans. Since 27 September 2026 an administrator may choose which of a language's two voices reads each presentation register — routine answers, navigation, the signed-out visitor and the administrator's own — and hear a sentence in it first; since 28 September 2026 which provider reads each presentation register and how, within the ceilings the same screen sets; and, inside the founder's signed-in session and there alone, the founder may enter, rotate, test and remove a provider's key on the box, switch a provider on or off and read its log, through the assistant service's own founder routes. The emergency, refusal and escalation registers stay locked. Every other action is disabled, beside the gate that holds it: there is no key vault, no per-tenant scoping, no health-check runner, no tenant and no kill switch, so nothing here can scope a key, add a provider, spend money beyond a heard preview, or switch the assistant off.
gilbertone._subScreensWhy: The seven sub-screens of §7, each with the contract it reads, the gate it stands behind and the file that draws it — except that §7's Voice is Speech settings since the founder's instruction of 28 September 2026 to collapse the two into one place: the merged screen stands where Voice stood, reads voice.json and stands behind G29, which holds the clinical-delivery register it draws locked. G33, which the separate Speech settings screen stood behind, still holds the offshore providers it offers and is the gate its provider rows name. The category's tabs above are these seven in this order, and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds the two lists to each other and every file to a dynamic import of its own.

gates.label: Gate G29
gates.sentence: Not available while gate G29 is open. Nobody clinical has reviewed the clinical-delivery register, so the voice that reads an emergency, a refusal or an escalation is read here and set by nobody: it changes only through a ratified entry in the Clinician Review Queue.

gates.label: Gate G30
gates.sentence: Not available while gate G30 is open. There is no key vault, so no key can be entered, rotated, tested or described here; and there is no per-tenant scoping, no residency decision and no DPIA per provider behind any of them.

gates.label: Gate G31
gates.sentence: Not available while gate G31 is open. No tenant exists to set a level or a ceiling for, and no clinician session exists to test the clinical-assist lock against, so every level on this screen is read and none is set.

gates.label: Gate G32
gates.sentence: Not available while gate G32 is open. There is no secret vault, no health-check runner and no enable, disable or balance control behind any card, so none of these actions can do anything.

gates.label: Module 8
gates.sentence: Not available: Module 8, the per-tenant kill switch, does not exist. There is no tenant to switch and nothing that could switch one. Today the assistant goes dark only when somebody at a terminal on the server stops it, and that is recorded by hand in docs/governance/ASSISTANT-ACTIVATION.md.

gates.label: Gate G33
gates.sentence: Open while gate G33 is open. A provider with no South African region — ElevenLabs, Alibaba Qwen — may be chosen for a register here and is refused by the service in production until the residency decision the responsible party and the Information Officer sign is recorded: the platform default reads the answer instead, and the refusal is printed at start-up.

gilbertone._gatesWhy: The refusal each disabled action shows, one per gate. A G-numbered gate is open while packages/catalog/control-tower-overview.json#open-gates records it open; Module 8 has no row in either register, so it is open while the tenancy contract and the kill switch's runtime it would need are both missing. scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails the build if a gate an action names is no longer open, because then the action is drawn disabled for a reason that has stopped being true and somebody has to build what it would do. An action the founder has made live carries gate null and a live record instead — who decided it, on which day, and the one sentence saying what it does and what it never does — and the build refuses a live action without all three, or one that still names a gate. An action the founder took for the founder alone, on 28 September 2026, carries gate null and a founder record of the same three parts instead: it is enabled only inside the founder's signed-in session, disabled beside the founder words below otherwise, and calls the assistant service's founder routes and nothing else. G29 holds no action since 27 September 2026: it still holds the clinical-delivery register, which no action on the Speech settings screen touches. G30 and G32 still hold what has no contract — scoping a key, adding a provider, testing every provider at once, the local agent — and are still open.

actions.label: Revert a tenant to the deterministic layer

live.sentence: Keeps the chosen voice, and since 28 September 2026 the chosen provider, for one presentation register as a setting in the assistant's history — who, when and why — and the next spoken answer in that register reads in it. Inside the founder's signed-in session the history is the assistant service's own; otherwise it is this tab's. It never touches the emergency, refusal or escalation register, which has no setting to save into, and it is not a person's chooser: no patient sees a voice list.

Keeps the knobs changed in one group — Azure Speech's, ElevenLabs', or the ceilings, timeouts, fallback and own voice every provider shares — as settings in the assistant's history, one change each with the same reason, and the next spoken answer of a presentation register is read with them. It never reaches an emergency, refusal or escalation answer, which is read with no knob whatever is saved, and it never holds a key or a region, which are not settings.

Reads the sentence typed here through the assistant service's own speak route, in the chosen language and voice, and shows the estimated cost before it does. It refuses text that looks like a person's details, never sends anything but that sentence, keeps no audio, and reads a locked register in the platform's own voice whatever any setting says.

founder.sentence: Sends the key typed here once to the assistant service, inside the founder's signed-in session and with a fresh authenticator code, to be held on the box for this provider. The field is cleared as it is sent; the answer is the key's last four characters and fingerprint, never the key; and nothing here stores, logs or echoes what was typed.

Opens the key field for this provider so a new key can be entered in place of the one on the box. It never shows the key in force — the old key's last four and fingerprint stay readable for the audit — and revoking the old key at the provider is done in the provider's own console, never here.

Asks the assistant service to remove this provider's key from the box, with a fresh authenticator code. The service decides what may be removed and answers in its own sentence; nothing here removes anything the service refuses, and a removed key is never shown as if it were still present.

Asks the assistant service to make one minimal call to this provider with the key on the box, and says whether it answered. It never sends a patient's words, never spends beyond that one call, and never shows the key.

Shows, for each provider the assistant service holds a key slot for, whether a key is set on the box, its last four characters and its SHA-256 fingerprint prefix, read from the service inside the founder's session. It never shows the key, and it never reads anything from the browser.

actions.label: Switch a tenant to the deterministic layer

founder.sentence: Asks the assistant service to switch this provider on, with a fresh authenticator code, and the service records who and why. It never switches on a provider the service refuses — one with no key on the box, or one the residency decision does not admit — and the card's state stays the registry's, not this button's.

Asks the assistant service to switch this provider off, with a fresh authenticator code. Every route that depends on it returns to the safe state the registry records; it never touches a key on the box or money already spent, and it never switches off the deterministic layer that answers when everything else is dark.

Opens the key field for this card so a new key can be entered in place of the one on the box, sent once with a fresh authenticator code and cleared as it goes. It never shows the key in force, and revoking the old key at the provider is done in the provider's own console, never here.

Asks the assistant service to make one minimal call to this provider with the key on the box, and says whether it answered. It never sends a patient's words, never spends beyond that one call, and never shows the key.

Reads this provider's own audit lines from the assistant service inside the founder's session — key events, tests and switches, each with when and its outcome. It never carries a patient's words, a key or a code, and nothing read here is kept.

gilbertone._actionsWhy: Every control a GilbertOne screen draws that would change something, with the gate that holds it, the founder's record that made it live, or the founder's record that made it the founder's alone. A screen draws an action only by naming it here. A gated action is drawn disabled with the gate's sentence (or the action's own refusal, where it has one) tied to it by aria-describedby — a disabled button with no sentence is skipped by some screen readers and says nothing about why. A live action is drawn enabled with its live sentence tied to it the same way, so the person pressing it reads what it does and what it never does. A founder action (28 September 2026) is drawn enabled only while the assistant service says the founder is signed in, described by its founder sentence, and disabled beside founder.words otherwise; it calls the founder routes founder.routes names and nothing else, and the build refuses one drawn any other way. The six card actions are api-registry.json#actions, each named by its registryAction; configure-scopes has no contract behind it and stays gated, and the card says so.

overview._fieldsWhy: The boolean fields both built routes return (packages/catalog/apis/assistant.json), and nothing else: not mode, which is a string, and nothing the routes might grow. Each is read as true only if the answer holds the boolean true, so a field that arrives as anything else is drawn as not, never as its value.
overview.notAnswered: The route did not answer. Nothing below it is read from the service.
overview.versionEmpty: No screen can read which build the service is running, when it was last deployed or when it last restarted. Deploys and restarts happen at a terminal on the server, and the restarts seen so far are written down by hand in docs/governance/ASSISTANT-ACTIVATION.md.
overview.acknowledgedSentence: Written by hand on the server when activated answers yes; this screen cannot read the file it is written in, only the route's answer.
overview.speechRegionSentence: Pinned in code to South Africa, so audio cannot be sent to another region; a pinned region is not a residency decision.
overview.refreshEmpty: No refresh of either corpus is recorded anywhere this screen can read, so there is no last refresh to show.

voice.lockedRowSentence: Changes only through a ratified entry in the Clinician Review Queue.
voice.previewTextHint: Typed here, kept in this screen only, and never sent anywhere.
voice.previewCostLabel: Estimated cost and speed, shown before Play
voice.previewTotalEmpty: Nothing has been played in this session, so the running total is nothing.
voice.previewAccepted: Nothing in this sentence looks like a person's details.
voice._previewRouteWhy: The one route Play asks, since the founder's decision of 27 September 2026: the assistant service's own speak route, at the built version packages/catalog/apis/assistant.json declares, under the same prefix the Overview reads. It is the patients' route — there is still no speak route an administrator signs in to — and the preview sends it nothing but the administrator's own sentence, the language, the contract's voice name and — since version four, 28 September 2026 — the register the sentence is read as, so the reading goes through the provider and tuning the administrator's settings name for that register. scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds lib/gilbertone-admin.ts to this path and to no other request but the two status reads.
voice.previewCostSentence: {characters} characters at {price} per {unit} characters — {provider}'s list price, recorded by hand on {recordedOn}, not a measurement — is about {cost}. Nothing has been timed, so no speed is shown.
voice.previewCostEmpty: Type a sentence to see what reading it would cost.
voice.previewTotalSentence: {plays} read this session, about {cost} in all.
voice.previewCeilingSentence: {read} of this session's ceiling of {ceiling} characters read.
voice.previewCeilingReached: This sentence would take the session past its preview ceiling of {ceiling} characters, so Play stays shut. The ceiling is an administrator's setting; a new session starts the count again.
voice._previewCostDecimalsWhy: Azure prices text to speech per million characters, so one sentence costs a fraction of a cent; a currency figure rounded to two places would show nothing and read as free. Five places show the fraction.
voice.previewReading: Asking the service to read it.
voice.previewNotAnswered: The service did not answer, so nothing was read and nothing was billed.
voice.previewNotPlayed: The service answered and the browser could not play the audio. The provider billed the reading all the same.
voice.previewOnlyThrough: A preview reads through {provider}, the one text-to-speech provider that is built and configured. Nothing here calls {card}, so there is nothing to play on this card.
voice.sessionSentence: Outside the founder's signed-in session a saved voice is kept in this tab's memory and nowhere else, beside every other setting on the Configuration screen; the shipped default is the contract's, and a reload puts it back. Inside it, the assistant service keeps the change in its own history and reads it for the next spoken answer.
voice.nothingToSave: The voice shown is the one in force, so there is nothing to save.

modelProviders.keyRegistryEmpty: There is no key metadata to show from a registry, because none exists: the vault and the metadata store the plan names are named-but-absent. No field on this screen accepts a key. None displays one, except founder access below, which shows the two Azure keys to the signed-in founder alone.
modelProviders.keyEntryHeading: Entering a key, as the contract draws it

intelligence.founderNote: The levels and the ceilings are not among the assistant engine's settings the founder's routes carry, so nothing here is the founder's to set yet: a level or a ceiling becomes a founder setting the day it is a setting in packages/catalog/intelligence-levels.json with a reader behind it, and until then the selector stays gated and says so.

speech.inForceHeading: In force for each presentation register
speech.editorIntro: The same editor as the Configuration tab, over the same rules and the same history: every change says why, is reviewed before it is confirmed, and is kept with who made it. In this preview a change is kept in this tab's memory for the session, and the shipped default is the contract's.
speech.residencySentence: No South African region. In production the service refuses it for a patient's voice until the residency decision is signed, and reads through {default} instead.
speech.onshoreSentence: Pinned to a South African region: the platform default, and the one provider that answers in production today.
speech.notExercisedSentence: Written from the vendor's published reference and not yet tried against the live API: the first operator to configure it finds out.
speech.noPriceSentence: No per-character list price is recorded, so the preview has nothing to multiply and will not play through it.
speech.serviceReadsDefaults: Outside the founder's signed-in session the assistant service reads every setting on this screen from the contract's defaults, as far as this screen can tell: it cannot read the service's history without the founder's session, so a change made here as a preview reaches the web preview and the next spoken answer in this tab, and never a patient. That is said here rather than hidden.
speech.changeHeading: Change the voice and the speech settings
speech.changeIntro: Choose, say why, and save. Each presentation register is saved on its own — its provider and its voice — and each group of knobs on its own. The rules and the refusals are the shared settings code's, and every change is kept with who made it, when and why.
speech.nothingChanged: Nothing shown differs from what is in force, so there is nothing to save.
speech.sourceService: In force on the assistant service: settings version {version}, read from the service's own history when this screen opened and again after every save. A change saved here is the service's, and the next spoken answer of a presentation register reads with it.
speech.sourceTab: In force in this tab's memory: settings version {version}. Founder access is not switched on here, so a change is a preview that reaches no patient, and a reload puts the contract's defaults back.
speech.sourceLocked: Shown below: the contract's shipped defaults. What the assistant service holds is read once the founder is signed in, and nothing here can be changed until then.
speech.sourceReading: Reading what the assistant service holds…

founder.instruction: API Registry, Compliance, Intelligence, Model Providers — I cannot set them. I need to be able to control all these aspects, I am the owner.
founder.why: The founder holds the Azure resources, the ElevenLabs account and the box, and is the one person who enters, rotates or removes a key or switches a provider today (docs/governance/FOUNDER-ACCESS.md). Until 28 September 2026 every such control was drawn disabled behind G30 or G32, because no vault and no runner existed; the founder's session, the service's founder routes and the founder's own instruction are what now stand behind exactly the actions above that carry a founder record. Each is enabled only while the assistant service says the founder is signed in, calls the service's founder routes and nothing else, sends a key once in a body and clears the field as it goes, and shows metadata and never a value. What still has no contract — scoping a key, adding a provider, testing every provider at once, the local agent, a reasoning level, a compliance sign-off — stays gated, and the screen says so where it is drawn.
founder._routesWhy: The assistant service's founder routes for settings and providers are founder-access.json's — settings, settingsChanges, providers, providerKey, providerEnabled, providerTest and providerLogs, under its prefix — each refusing without the founder's session cookie and the founder header (founder-access.json#request), and the key, enabled and remove routes each asking a fresh authenticator code as a reveal does. Their request and response fields are packages/catalog/apis/assistant.json's; apps/web/src/lib/founder-settings.ts reads only the fields it names and never a key, and every path is read from that contract, never typed on a screen or copied here.

compliance.auditEmpty: The audit extract is for layer 13, the Auditor, and for nobody else. No session exists that could say somebody is layer 13, so this panel shows nothing to anybody. When it exists it is a read-only view of the append-only store, filtered by date range, tenant and event type.
compliance.residencyObserved: Observed on the server, not decided
compliance.founderNote: Nothing on this screen is the founder's to sign yet. A sign-off — who signed, when and why — needs a contract naming what is being signed, and none of the six sections, the audit extract or the kill switch has one; the day one does, it is recorded against the founder's session like every other founder action, and never as a button that says it did something.

gilbertone.why: §4, §7 and §10 Phase 4: GilbertOne API Administration, built against contracts and the service's own health and status routes, with the vault, the key registry and the health-check runner still named-but-absent. The screens can be built against a stub; the live path waits for G30 and G32, and this category says so rather than drawing the wireframes' values.

tree.label: Sites
tree.emptyState: No site exists. MyThuso has no site registry: every visit, nurse and device in this preview belongs to one operation with no site boundary. A site is created by a tenancy contract naming what one is, and that contract does not exist.

tree.label: Wards
tree.emptyState: No ward exists, because no site exists to hold one. Wards are the hospital shape the plan describes; nothing in the tree models a hospital floor yet.

tree.label: Beds
tree.emptyState: No bed exists, because no ward exists to hold one. A bed is also the first axis of cost allocation, which is why that axis is empty too.

tree.label: Staff
tree.emptyState: No tenant has its own staff directory, because no tenant exists. The people this preview knows are parties on the vetting register, and they are read and decided on in Vetting.

tree.label: Roles
tree.emptyState: No admin role exists. The roles below open screens and grant nothing; the fifteen admin layers the plan describes are named-but-absent until gate G16.

tree.label: Branding
tree.emptyState: One brand, fixed. The token palette in packages/design-tokens/tokens.json governs every screen, and no tenant may override it; per-tenant branding needs a tenant, and none exists.

tree.label: Integrations
tree.emptyState: No integration is connected: {connected} of {total} capabilities in packages/catalog/capabilities.json. Each one below is simulated or absent, and says so on the screens that depend on it.

configuration._treeWhy: §6.2: Configuration becomes the tenant-admin home, a tree of sites, wards, beds, staff, roles, branding and integrations, each with its own sub-screen and its own empty state. The existing settings screen stays reachable as the tree's first node, so nothing that was on the Configuration tab moved away from it.

costAllocation.refusal: No cost figure is shown until a meter exists behind it. The period chosen above changes nothing here, for the same reason.

reviewQueue.noSignature: Nothing on this screen signs, ratifies, rejects or rolls back. The governance board is {board} and the Medical Director is {director}, so no signature exists to give — for anybody.
reviewQueue.why: §6.2: Governance gains the Clinician Review Queue. The queue's contract is proposed and has no runtime, no route and no entry; the screen reads the contract and the governance record it names, and offers no action while the board is not formed.

refusals.statement: The portal claims no permission. A category being on the screen does not mean anybody may use it; nothing here is reached by having permission to.
refusals.why: Default-deny (§1) has no allow to invert while there is no session. Saying so is the control that exists.

refusals.statement: Nothing in the portal enables a device class, pairs a device or assigns one.
refusals.why: §12: do not enable a device class at a site without a DPIA. The DPIA is not done.

refusals.statement: The review-queue screen offers no sign, ratify, reject or roll-back action while the governance board is not formed.
refusals.why: packages/catalog/clinical-review-queue.json#no-signature-no-ratification: a ratification that cannot say whose authority it was is citing nobody.

refusals.statement: No cost allocation figure is drawn until a meter exists behind it.
refusals.why: A cost per bed with no bed and no meter is an invented number on a finance screen.

refusals.statement: No GilbertOne administration action does anything while its gate is open. Each is drawn disabled, beside the sentence that names the gate holding it and why.
refusals.why: §9: nothing in this phase is built as more than documentation until its gate is green. The assistant is live in production, and a control on its administration screen that looked as if it worked would be the most dangerous thing in the portal to mistake for real. Replaced, on 24 September 2026 in Phase 4, the refusal no-gilbertone-sub-screen-before-phase-4, which Phase 4 retired by building the sub-screens. Since 27 September 2026 an action the founder made live carries a dated live record in place of a gate — the Speech settings screen's Save as default, Save and Play — and since 28 September 2026 an action the founder took for the founder alone carries a founder record instead; this refusal holds every action that still names a gate.

refusals.statement: An action the founder made the founder's on 28 September 2026 is enabled only while the assistant service says the founder is signed in, and calls the service's founder routes and nothing else. Signed out it is disabled beside the sentence that says so. A key it sends goes once, in the body of one request, and the field is cleared as it goes; what comes back is the key's last four characters and fingerprint, never the key, and nothing is stored, logged or put in an address.
refusals.why: The founder's instruction — "I need to be able to control all these aspects, I am the owner" — is met by the founder's session and the service's routes, not by the browser trusting itself. The browser draws what the service decided; the service refuses without the cookie, the header and, for a key, a switch or a removal, a fresh authenticator code.

refusals.statement: No administration screen accepts, shows or keeps a key, a fragment of one or a deployment's address, with one exception: founder access, through which the founder alone — signed in with a password and an authenticator code, while the service has it switched on by hand — may reveal the two Azure keys, one at a time, with a fresh code. The only key-entry field drawn is the founder's, inside a signed-in founder session, posted once to the assistant service and cleared as it is sent; the metadata shown is what the service answers, and there is no key registry beyond it.
refusals.why: §1: API keys never reach the browser. The vault is the security boundary and does not exist, so the honest screen is one with nowhere to type a key and nothing about one to read.

preview: The portal is the two old surfaces' screens, unchanged, under one navigation, with six new screens that are each a written empty state or a contract read aloud — the Overview, Devices & Fleet, the Configuration tree, cost allocation, the compliance pack preview and the Clinician Review Queue — and, since Phase 4, GilbertOne API Administration's seven sub-screens, whose every action is disabled beside its gate but the ones the founder made live: a presentation voice and provider chosen and saved as a setting, the knobs saved beside them, a sentence heard first, and — inside the founder's signed-in session alone — a provider's key entered, rotated, tested or removed, a provider switched on or off and its log read, through the assistant service's founder routes. Nothing else in it acts on a real service.
